ecg-tachy-061.question: A 60-year-old man has a radial pulse of 38 bpm, whereas the monitor displays 76 bpm. How should the rhythm on this tracing be described?
options: 2:1 AV block with bundle branch block
commentaires: Incorrect: no premature P wave precedes the wide complexes.
Correct: each sinus QRS is followed by a wide PVC with no P wave; the haemodynamically ineffective PVCs explain the pulse deficit.
Incorrect: the wide complexes are premature and are not preceded by any conducted P wave.
Incorrect: at least 3 consecutive ventricular complexes are needed; here they alternate with sinus beats.
ecg-tachy-061.explication: On this tracing each narrow sinus QRS is followed by a wide, premature QRS not preceded by a P wave. A premature ventricular contraction is a premature, wide (> 120 ms) QRS, differing in morphology from the baseline QRS, not preceded by a premature P wave, with a T wave of opposite polarity. When every sinus beat is followed by a PVC, this is ventricular bigeminy. Atrial bigeminy consists of premature complexes preceded by a premature P wave, usually with narrow QRS complexes. Non-sustained VT requires at least 3 consecutive ventricular complexes. The manually counted pulse is falsely low here, because early PVCs are haemodynamically ineffective.
ecg-tachy-061.aRetenir: A PVC after every sinus QRS = ventricular bigeminy.

ecg-tachy-062.question: A 50-year-old woman reports a sensation of "thumps" in her chest. How should the premature beats on this tracing be interpreted?
commentaires: Correct: premature P wave of different morphology, followed by a narrow QRS identical to the baseline QRS.
Incorrect: a PVC would be wide, with no premature P wave.
Incorrect: a capture beat is only meaningful during ventricular tachycardia or AV dissociation.
Incorrect: an escape beat occurs late, after a pause; these beats are premature.
ecg-tachy-062.explication: On this tracing the premature beats have a narrow QRS identical to the baseline QRS and are preceded by a P wave of different morphology. A premature atrial contraction is recognised by a premature P wave whose morphology differs from the sinus P wave (because it arises elsewhere in the atrium), usually followed by a narrow QRS identical to the baseline QRS. The ensuing pause is usually non-compensatory, because the PAC penetrates and "resets" the sinus node. A PVC is wide, with no premature P wave. An escape beat is late, not premature. A very early PAC may be blocked (no QRS) or conducted with aberrancy (wide QRS), two common pitfalls.
ecg-tachy-062.aRetenir: PAC = premature P wave of different morphology, usually a narrow QRS.

ecg-tachy-063.question: Why is a premature ventricular contraction classically followed by a fully compensatory pause?
options: It resets the sinus node retrogradely
It causes transient complete AV block
It transiently blocks the right bundle branch
It does not reset the sinus node
commentaires: Incorrect: this is the mechanism of a PAC, which explains its non-compensatory pause.
Incorrect: the non-conducted P wave is blocked by physiological refractoriness, not by pathological AV block.
Incorrect: the compensatory pause does not depend on bundle branch block.
Correct: the sinus node continues at its own rate; the next P wave, falling in the refractory period, is not conducted: exactly 2 cycles.
ecg-tachy-063.explication: A PVC is not usually conducted retrogradely as far as the sinus node, which continues to fire at its own rate. The sinus P wave occurring during or just after the PVC finds the AV node or the ventricles refractory and is not conducted; the next sinus beat therefore arrives on time. The interval between the QRS preceding and the QRS following the PVC is then exactly two sinus cycles: this is the fully compensatory pause. A PAC usually resets the sinus node, hence a non-compensatory pause. A PVC can also be interpolated (with no pause) when the sinus rate is slow.
ecg-tachy-063.aRetenir: PVC: fully compensatory pause (2 sinus cycles); PAC: non-compensatory pause.

ecg-tachy-064.question: A Holter recording shows several pauses with no QRS. On close inspection, the T wave preceding each pause is deformed (notched) compared with the other T waves. What is the most likely explanation?
commentaires: Correct: the premature, non-conducted P wave is superimposed on the preceding T wave, which it deforms.
Incorrect: a sinus pause is not accompanied by deformation of the preceding T wave.
Incorrect: in Mobitz II the blocked P wave occurs on time and remains visible; it does not deform the T wave.
Incorrect: no pacemaker is mentioned; the deformed T wave indicates a premature P wave.
ecg-tachy-064.explication: A very early PAC can occur while the AV node is still refractory: it is not conducted to the ventricles. Its premature P wave is superimposed on the preceding T wave, which it deforms. The ensuing pause is often mistaken for a sinus pause or AV block. A blocked PAC is the most common cause of an unexplained pause on a Holter recording. In Mobitz II, blocked P waves occur on time (constant PP interval), not prematurely. Comparing T-wave morphology should be a reflex whenever a pause is seen.
ecg-tachy-064.aRetenir: Pause preceded by a deformed T wave = blocked PAC.

ecg-tachy-065.question: Ashman phenomenon is the aberrant conduction, usually with an RBBB-like pattern, of a supraventricular complex occurring after a long–short cycle sequence.
commentaires: Correct: the refractory period depends on the preceding cycle; after a long cycle, an early complex finds the right bundle branch refractory.
Incorrect: the statement is true; it is a classic cause of a wide complex wrongly taken for a PVC in AF.
ecg-tachy-065.explication: The refractory period of the His–Purkinje system depends on the length of the preceding cycle: the longer the preceding cycle, the longer the subsequent refractory period. A premature complex following a long cycle may therefore find a bundle branch still refractory, most often the right bundle branch (which has the longest refractory period), hence an RBBB-like pattern. This phenomenon is common in AF, where it is often wrongly taken for PVCs. The absence of a compensatory pause and a typical bundle branch block morphology favour aberrancy.
ecg-tachy-065.aRetenir: Ashman: long then short cycle → aberrant complex (RBBB-like), not to be mistaken for a PVC.

ecg-tachy-066.question: A patient has an unexplained LVEF of 35% (normal coronary arteries, no late gadolinium enhancement on MRI) and monomorphic PVCs on Holter. According to the 2022 ESC guidelines, above which burden should PVC-induced cardiomyopathy be suspected?
commentaires: Incorrect: a 1% burden does not explain LV dysfunction.
Incorrect: a 5% burden is rarely sufficient to explain LV dysfunction.
Correct: ESC 2022, suspect PVC-induced cardiomyopathy from a burden of 10% (IIa).
Incorrect: far too high a threshold; the risk appears from 10%, often > 20% in published series.
ecg-tachy-066.explication: The 2022 ESC guidelines recommend that PVC-induced cardiomyopathy be suspected in a patient with unexplained LV dysfunction and a PVC burden of at least 10% of beats (class IIa). The risk increases with burden (often > 20% in published series), but also with PVC width, epicardial origin and interpolation. The diagnosis is confirmed retrospectively by improvement in LVEF after PVC suppression (first-line ablation or antiarrhythmic drug). A burden of 1 to 5% is rarely sufficient to explain LV dysfunction.
ecg-tachy-066.aRetenir: Unexplained LV dysfunction + PVCs ≥ 10%: think arrhythmia-induced cardiomyopathy and consider ablation.

ecg-tachy-067.question: Which ECG appearance defines the type 1 Brugada pattern?
options: Saddleback ST elevation ≥ 2 mm with a positive T in V1–V2
Epsilon wave and negative T waves in V1–V3
Coved ST elevation ≥ 2 mm followed by a negative T in V1 or V2
Diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression
commentaires: Incorrect: this is type 2 (saddleback), which is only suggestive and requires a search for a type 1 pattern.
Incorrect: an epsilon wave and negative T waves in V1–V3 suggest arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy.
Correct: convex, downsloping ST elevation ≥ 2 mm followed by a negative T wave in V1 and/or V2: the only diagnostic pattern.
Incorrect: this picture suggests acute pericarditis.
ecg-tachy-067.explication: The type 1 Brugada pattern combines, in V1 and/or V2 (recorded in the 2nd, 3rd or 4th intercostal spaces), J-point/ST elevation ≥ 2 mm that is downsloping and convex ("coved"), followed by a negative T wave. It is the only diagnostic pattern. Type 2 (saddleback) is merely suggestive and requires a drug challenge to unmask a type 1 pattern. An epsilon wave is a sign of ARVC. Diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression suggests pericarditis. Recording V1–V2 in a high position increases sensitivity.
ecg-tachy-067.aRetenir: Type 1 Brugada: coved ST ≥ 2 mm + negative T in V1–V2 (including high-placed leads).

ecg-tachy-068.question: Which factors can unmask or aggravate a type 1 Brugada pattern?
commentaires: Correct: fever further reduces the sodium current; it must be treated promptly in these patients.
Correct: used as a diagnostic challenge to unmask a type 1 pattern.
Incorrect: isoprenaline is used to treat electrical storm in Brugada syndrome.
Incorrect: quinidine (an Ito blocker) is a treatment for Brugada syndrome.
ecg-tachy-068.explication: Brugada syndrome is most often related to a reduced sodium current (SCN5A). Anything that further reduces this current accentuates the ECG pattern and the arrhythmic risk: fever (so much so that fever must be treated promptly in these patients), sodium channel blockers (used as a diagnostic challenge: ajmaline, flecainide), certain psychotropic drugs, anaesthetic agents, alcohol and cocaine. Vagal tone (rest, sleep, large meals) also accentuates the pattern. Conversely, isoprenaline and quinidine (which blocks the Ito current) are used to treat electrical storm. The list of drugs to avoid is kept up to date on dedicated databases.
ecg-tachy-068.aRetenir: Brugada: fever and sodium channel blockers unmask; isoprenaline and quinidine treat.

ecg-tachy-069.question: According to the 2022 ESC guidelines, a spontaneous type 2 ("saddleback") Brugada pattern is sufficient to diagnose Brugada syndrome.
commentaires: Incorrect: only the type 1 pattern, spontaneous or unmasked, is diagnostic.
Correct: a type 2 pattern calls for a search for a type 1 pattern (high lead placement, drug challenge, ECG during fever).
ecg-tachy-069.explication: Only the type 1 pattern, spontaneous or unmasked, is diagnostic. A type 2 pattern calls for a search for a type 1 pattern (high lead placement, ajmaline or flecainide challenge, ECG during fever). According to the 2022 ESC guidelines, a spontaneous type 1 pattern is sufficient for the diagnosis in the absence of other heart disease. By contrast, a type 1 pattern induced only by a sodium channel blocker requires at least one additional feature (arrhythmic syncope or nocturnal agonal respiration, family history of Brugada syndrome or of sudden death at a young age with a negative autopsy). This limits false positives related to the drug challenge.
ecg-tachy-069.aRetenir: Brugada: only type 1 is diagnostic; an induced type 1 pattern requires an additional clinical criterion.

ecg-tachy-070.question: Measured QT 400 ms, RR interval 640 ms (HR ≈ 94 bpm). What is the QTc according to Bazett?
commentaires: Incorrect: this is the raw, uncorrected QT.
Incorrect: this value does not correspond to any standard formula; Fridericia would give about 465 ms.
Incorrect: the classic error of dividing by the RR (400/0.64) instead of by its square root.
ecg-tachy-070.explication: The Bazett formula is QTc = QT / √RR (RR in seconds). Here √0.64 = 0.8, so QTc = 400 / 0.8 = 500 ms, which is clearly prolonged. The classic error is to divide by the RR rather than by its square root (400/0.64 = 625 ms). Bazett, however, overcorrects at high heart rates: at 94 bpm the value obtained may overestimate the QTc, and the Fridericia formula (cube root) gives about 465 ms here. A borderline QTc at a fast rate should therefore be interpreted with caution and, if possible, rechecked at a slower rate.
ecg-tachy-070.aRetenir: Bazett: QTc = QT/√RR (in seconds); beware of overcorrection during tachycardia.

ecg-tachy-071.question: Why is the Fridericia formula often preferred to Bazett in a tachycardic patient (e.g. in fast AF or on a drug that can cause torsades)?
options: Bazett undercorrects the QTc at high heart rates
Bazett overcorrects the QTc at high heart rates
Fridericia is the only formula validated in women
Fridericia does not require the RR to be measured
commentaires: Incorrect: it is the opposite; Bazett undercorrects at slow heart rates.
Correct: during tachycardia, Bazett overestimates the QTc and can lead to a wrong conclusion of long QT.
Incorrect: no formula has this status; the choice depends on rate dependence.
Incorrect: all correction formulae require measurement of the RR.
ecg-tachy-071.explication: The Bazett correction (QT/√RR) excessively lengthens the QTc at high heart rates and shortens it at slow rates. During tachycardia it can therefore lead to a wrong conclusion of long QT, resulting in unnecessary discontinuation of treatment. The Fridericia formula (QT/∛RR) and linear formulae (Framingham, Hodges) are less rate-dependent. The AHA/ACCF/HRS recommendations on ECG standardisation highlight these limitations and advise using a linear correction. All formulae require measurement of the RR.
ecg-tachy-071.aRetenir: Bazett overcorrects during tachycardia: prefer Fridericia or a linear formula.

ecg-tachy-072.question: Congenital long QT: bifid, low-amplitude T wave, with syncopal episodes triggered by an alarm clock. Which genotype is most likely?
commentaires: Incorrect: LQT1 produces a broad T wave and events on exertion, particularly swimming.
Incorrect: LQT3 produces a long isoelectric ST segment and events at rest or during sleep.
Incorrect: a recessive form with congenital deafness, not suggested here.
Correct: low-amplitude, bifid T waves and events triggered by sudden auditory stimuli.
ecg-tachy-072.explication: The three main genotypes have fairly typical profiles. LQT2 (KCNH2, IKr current) produces low-amplitude, bifid or notched T waves, with events triggered by sudden auditory stimuli (alarm clock, telephone) or in the postpartum period. LQT1 (KCNQ1, IKs) produces a broad-based T wave, with events on exertion, particularly swimming. LQT3 (SCN5A, late sodium current) combines a long isoelectric ST segment followed by a late T wave, with events at rest or during sleep. Jervell and Lange-Nielsen syndrome is a recessive form with congenital deafness.
ecg-tachy-072.aRetenir: LQT1: exertion/swimming; LQT2: bifid T, auditory stimuli; LQT3: rest/sleep.
